'''David X. Li''' ({{lang-zh|s=李祥林|p=Lǐ Xiánglín}}<ref name="Jones" /> born [[Nanjing, China]] in the 1960s) is a Chinese-born Canadian [[quantitative analyst]] and [[actuary]] who pioneered the use of [[Gaussian copula]] models for the pricing of [[collateralized debt obligation]]s (CDOs) in the early 2000s.<ref name="Salmon">{{cite journal |journal=Wired Magazine |date=March 2009 |volume=17 |issue=3 |url=https://www.wired.com/techbiz/it/magazine/17-03/wp_quant |title=Recipe for Disaster: The Formula That Killed Wall Street |first=Felix |last=Salmon |author-link=Felix Salmon |publisher=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]}}</ref><ref name="Li">{{cite journal |doi=10.3905/jfi.2000.319253 |first=David X. |last=Li |year=2000 |url=http://www.defaultrisk.com/pp_corr_05.htm |title=On Default Correlation: A Copula Function Approach |journal=[[Journal of Fixed Income]] |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=43–54 |s2cid=167437822 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080430090434/http://www.defaultrisk.com/pp_corr_05.htm |archive-date=2008-04-30 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Kelly">{{cite news|last1=Kelly|first1=Cathal|author-link=Cathal Kelly|title=Meet the man whose big idea felled Wall Street|url=https://www.thestar.com/business/2009/03/18/meet_the_man_whose_big_idea_felled_wall_street.html|work=[[The Toronto Star]]|date=18 March 2009|language=en-CA}}</ref>  The ''[[Financial Times]]'' has called him "the world's most influential actuary",<ref name="Jones">{{Cite news |title=Of couples and copulas |url=https://www.ft.com/content/912d85e8-2d75-11de-9eba-00144feabdc0 |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090425011843/http://www.ft.com/cms/s/2/912d85e8-2d75-11de-9eba-00144feabdc0.html |archive-date=2009-04-25 |url-status=live |first=Sam |last=Jones |newspaper=[[Financial Times]] |date=April 24, 2009 }}</ref> while after the [[2008 financial crisis]], to which Li's model has been partly credited to blame,<ref name="Jones"/><ref name="Salmon"/> his model has been called a "recipe for disaster" in the hands of those who did not fully understand his research and misapplied it.<ref name="Salmon"/> Widespread application of simplified Gaussian copula models to [[financial products]] such as [[securities]] may have contributed to the [[2008 financial crisis]].<ref name="Salmon"/><ref>{{cite web|last1=Hornbrook|first1=Mike|title=Was David Li the guy who 'blew up Wall Street?'|url=http://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/was-david-li-the-guy-who-blew-up-wall-street-1.775732|website=CBC News Canada|ref=CBC}}</ref> David Li is currently an adjunct professor at the [[University of Waterloo]] in the Statistics and Actuarial Sciences department.<ref name="S&AS"/>

==Early life and education==
Li was born as Li Xianglin and raised in a rural part of [[China]] during the 1960s;<ref name="Salmon"/> his family had been relocated during the [[Cultural Revolution]] to a rural village in southern China for "re-education".<ref name="Jones" /> Li received a [[Master of Economics|master's degree in economics]] from [[Nankai University]].<ref name="Jones" /> After leaving China in 1987 at the behest of the Chinese government to study [[capitalism]] in [[Western world|Western society]],<ref name="Jones" /> he earned an [[Master of Business Administration|MBA]] from [[Laval University]] in [[Quebec]], a [[MMath]] in [[Actuarial Science]] and [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in statistics from the [[University of Waterloo]] in [[Waterloo, Ontario]]<ref name="Salmon"/> in 1995 with a thesis titled "''An estimating function approach to credibility theory"'' under the supervision of [[Harry Panjer]].<ref>{{cite web |url = https://www.proquest.com/docview/194155644/ |title = An estimating function approach to credibility theory  |first = Xianglin |last = Li|id={{ProQuest|194155644 }}}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://uwaterloo.ca/statistics-and-actuarial-science/about/people/harry-panjer|title=Harry Panjer|date=2015-02-20|work=Statistics and Actuarial Science|access-date=2018-03-21|language=en}}</ref>

== Career ==
Li began his career in finance in 1997 at the [[Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce]] in the World Markets division.<ref name="Salmon" /> He moved to [[New York City]] in 2000 where he became a partner in [[J.P. Morgan]]'s RiskMetrics unit.<ref name="Kelly" /> By 2003 he was director and global head of credit [[Derivative (finance)|derivatives]] research at [[Citigroup]].<ref name="Jones" /> In 2004 he moved to [[Barclays Capital]] and lead the credit [[Quantitative analyst|quantitative analytics]] team.<ref name="Salmon" /> In 2008 Li moved to [[Beijing]] where he worked for [[China International Capital Corporation]] as the head of the [[risk management]] department.<ref name="Salmon" />

David Li is currently an adjunct professor at the [[University of Waterloo]] in the Statistics and Actuarial Sciences department.<ref name="S&AS">{{cite web|title=David X. Li|url=https://uwaterloo.ca/statistics-and-actuarial-science/about/people/david-x-li|work=Statistics and Actuarial Science|location=University of Waterloo|language=en|date=23 February 2015}}</ref> He is also a professor at the [[Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance]] (SAIF).<ref name="S&AS" />

==CDOs and Gaussian copula==
Li's paper "On Default Correlation: A Copula Function Approach"<ref name="Li"/> was the first appearance of the [[Gaussian copula]] applied to CDOs published in 2000, which quickly became a tool for financial institutions to correlate associations between multiple financial [[Security (finance)|securities]].<ref name="Salmon"/> This allowed for CDOs to be supposedly accurately priced for a wide range of investments that were previously too complex to price, such as [[mortgages]].

However, after the [[2008 financial crisis]], the model has been seen as a "recipe for disaster".<ref name="Salmon"/> According to [[Nassim Nicholas Taleb]], "People got very excited about the Gaussian copula because of its mathematical elegance, but the thing never worked. Co-association between securities is not measurable using [[correlation]]"; in other words, "anything that relies on correlation is charlatanism."<ref name="Salmon"/>

Li himself apparently understood the fallacy of his model, in 2005 saying "Very few people understand the essence of the model."<ref name="Whitehouse" /> Li also wrote that "The current copula framework gains its popularity owing to its simplicity....However, there is little theoretical justification of the current framework from financial economics....We essentially have a credit portfolio model without solid credit portfolio theory."<ref>{{cite book |title=The Definitive Guide to CDOs: Market, Application, Valuation and Hedging |publisher=Risk Books |editor-first=Gunter |editor-last=Meissner |year=2008 |page=71 |isbn=9781906348014 }}</ref> Kai Gilkes of [[CreditSights]] says "Li can't be blamed"; although he invented the model, it was the bankers who misinterpreted and misused it.<ref name="Salmon"/>

===Li's paper===
Li's paper is called "On Default Correlation: A Copula Function Approach" (2000), published in ''[[Journal of Fixed Income]]'', Vol. 9, Issue 4, pages 43–54.<ref name="Whitehouse">{{Cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB112649094075137685|title=How a Formula Ignited Market That Burned Some Big Investors |first=Mark |last=Whitehouse |date=September 12, 2005 |newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]}} [https://web.archive.org/web/20090326130026/http://math.bu.edu/people/murad/MarkWhitehouseSlicesofRisk.txt Alt URL].</ref><ref name="Li"/> In section 1 through 5.3, Li describes actuarial math that sets the stage for his theory. The mathematics are from established statistical theory, actuarial models, and probability theory. In section 5.4, he uses [[Copula (statistics)#Gaussian copula|Gaussian copula]] to measure event relationships, or mathematically, ''correlations'', between random economic events, expressed as:

::<math>C_\rho(u,v) = \Phi \left(\Phi^{-1}(u), \Phi^{-1}(v); \rho \right) </math>

In layman's terms, he proposes to quantify the relationship between two events "House A" defaulting and "House B" defaulting by looking at the dependence between their time-unit-default (or  survival time; see [[survival analysis]]). While under some scenarios (such as real estate) this correlation appeared to work most of the time, the underlying problem is that the single numerical data of correlation is a poor way to summarize history, and hence is not enough to predict the future. From section 6.0 onward, the paper presents experimental results using the Gaussian copula.
